candidates.title: Responses of large language models to common questions on premature ovarian insufficiency: A comparative analysis
candidates.abstract: Abstract Objective Large language models are widely used in clinical care. Their reliability in specialized gynecological diseases such as premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) has not been fully verified. This study aimed to systematically evaluate and compare the accuracy and completeness of three mainstream large language models when answering standardized clinical questions about POI. Methods We developed 34 standardized questions covering five core domains of POI according to international clinical guidelines. Two senior obstetricians and gynecologists independently scored responses using a 5‐point Likert scale. Inter‐rater reliability was assessed using Cohen's kappa coefficient, intraclass correlation coefficient, and mean absolute error. Pairwise between‐model score differences were computed and visualized using item‐level heatmaps. Results All three models showed high and steady performance. Accuracy scores ranged from 4.59 to 4.84, and completeness scores ranged from 4.43 to 4.65. Inter‐rater agreement was “good” to “ excellent”, with exact agreement between 91.18% and 97.06% and Cohen's kappa between 0.675 and 0.915. GPT‐5.5 performed better in the area of clinical manifestations and treatment. DeepSeek‐R1 showed greater stability, defined as maintaining consistently high scores with limited score fluctuation, in etiology‐ and counseling‐related questions. Item‐level heatmaps revealed that most individual‐item differences were within ±0.5 points, whereas pairwise differences in overall mean scores fell within ±0.5, and some individual‐item comparisons exceeded this range, with no obvious systematic bias. Conclusions GPT‐5.5, Claude Opus‐4.7, and DeepSeek‐R1 demonstrated favorable accuracy and completeness in answering standardized POI questions; overall performance was similar despite deviations across several individual questions. Item‐level difference heatmaps further confirmed the consistency and reliability of the three models. These models can serve as reliable auxiliary tools for clinical information retrieval and patient education under professional supervision, meaning that all content generated by artificial intelligence must be checked by qualified clinicians before clinical use.

candidates.title: Performance of large language models in pediatric infectious disease education: a multi-condition comparative study
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background Evaluating how appropriate current large language models (LLMs) respond to common pediatric infectious disease (PID) questions is important for understanding their potential role in education and clinical support. Therefore, we evaluated and compared the clinical quality of answers produced by different LLMs when given professionally written, clinician-style case descriptions, using a purpose-built multi-domain evaluation tool. Methods Three different LLMs, including DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, ChatGPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, were investigated using 12 relevant PID scenarios. Each scenario included five open-ended questions: etiology, clinical features, diagnostics, treatment options, and complications. Two PID specialists independently reviewed all responses using a Likert scoring tool. Results All three models received high overall scores. ChatGPT-5 achieved perfect domain scores (10.0), whereas DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp showed similarly strong results, with only minor reductions in diagnostics (9.83) and treatment (9.92). Gemini 2.5 Flash demonstrated higher variability, particularly in treatment (8.83) and diagnostics (9.75), while matching the other models in clinical findings and complications (10.0) and scoring 9.83 in etiology. However, there were no statistically significant differences across models in domain-level comparisons (all p > 0.05). In addition, model-level analyses similarly demonstrated high accuracy (6.0; 5.98; 5.85), completeness (3.0; 2.97; 2.87), and safety (1.0; 1.0; 0.97) for ChatGPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, respectively (accuracy: p = 0.074; completeness: p = 0.066; safety: p = 0.14). Conclusion Current LLMs performed highly in structured, expert-reviewed PID scenarios and may assist with information organization and early-stage clinical reasoning. However, their optimal use remains within clinician-supervised workflows, where AI-generated outputs complement, rather than replace, human clinical judgment. Impact Current large language models (LLMs) show consistently high-quality performance across pediatric infectious disease scenarios, with no significant differences between models. Our study adds a structured, multi-domain comparison using clinician-style cases and expert evaluation, providing detailed insights into accuracy, completeness, and safety. The findings support the use of LLMs in medical education and early clinical reasoning, while highlighting their role as clinician-supervised tools rather than replacements for clinical judgment. The results demonstrate the reliability of LLMs in organizing clinical information and identifying key diagnostic and management elements in standardized scenarios.

candidates.title: Large language models for depression assessment from brief daily diaries
candidates.abstract: Abstract Closely tracking changes in depression is important for clinical research and practice. However, intensive longitudinal depression assessment relies on self-report surveys that have major limitations. Scoring depression from natural language with large language models (LLMs) could resolve these shortcomings. This study tested the validity of depression rated by LLMs from daily video diaries. We studied 108 participants selected for mental health treatment status (45% in treatment). Participants completed a clinical interview and 14-21 days of depression surveys and video diaries. Daily depression scores were estimated by LLMs from diary transcripts. LLM ratings converged with self-report depression within-person ( r = .45;95% CrI[.40, .49]) and when averaged across days for an overall depression score ( r = .61;95% CrI[.43,.75]). Averaged LLM ratings correlated with depression symptom severity ascertained by clinical interview ( r = .53;95% CrI[.35, .68]). LLM-rated depression and self-report had similar profiles of associations with daily functioning variables (profile r = .98 within-person; r = .94 between-person). Multivariable regression results showed LLM ratings predicted daily functioning variables (partial $$\beta s$$ β s =|.12 | - | .28 | ) and interview-rated depression (partial $$\beta$$ β =.33;95% CrI[.07, .58]) over and above self-reports, suggesting LLMs capture clinically-relevant information that self-reports miss. Findings establish a strong foundation for a depression assessment approach that addresses shortcomings of self-reports while satisfying the unique demands of intensive longitudinal monitoring.

candidates.title: Institutional Document Chatbots for User Support: A Critical Narrative Review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Accuracy, Grounding, and Hallucination
candidates.abstract: Institutional chatbots can retrieve regulations, service instructions, and frequently asked questions before generating responses. However, access to documents does not establish that an answer is correct, complete, current, or authorized. This critical narrative review asks whether document-grounded chatbots improve answer accuracy and reduce unsupported information compared with language models without institutional retrieval. Targeted scholarly web searches and primary-source verification were completed on October 15, 2026, with a targeted public-record verification on October 16, 2026. The original 20-source corpus was expanded to 23 sources: 20 research publications, one conference research abstract, one enterprise benchmark preprint, and one official risk-management publication. Evidence was separated into applied information-service studies, benchmark and component studies, evaluation methods, adversarial research, and governance guidance. Published applications support conditional improvements, while benchmarks demonstrate persistent failures in grounding, citation, rejection of unanswerable questions, and use of time-sensitive or sparse private evidence. No common effect size was calculated because comparators, questions, models, and outcome definitions differ. Accuracy, source faithfulness, completeness, citation validity, temporal applicability, and authorized disclosure and verified task resolution must be evaluated separately. The review proposes an unvalidated institutional evaluation protocol using matched questions, a fixed model, independent document-based reference answers, blinded assessment, and explicit abstention denominators. The literature supports carefully governed RAG as a means of improving bounded institutional assistance; it does not establish universal superiority or elimination of hallucinations. Local comparative testing, Portuguese-language validation, document lifecycle management, and measurement of total user and staff effort remain necessary before deployment claims can be justified.

candidates.title: Effect of hierarchical prompt engineering on convolutional neural networks generated by large language models for helmet wearing compliance classification
candidates.abstract: Abstract Non-compliance with Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) use regulations, particularly helmet wearing, remains a critical occupational safety challenge in high-risk industrial environments. This study investigates how hierarchical prompt engineering shapes the quality of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) for image-level helmet-wearing compliance classification (helmet vs. no-helmet) as a mechanism for PPE compliance monitoring. Four LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok) produced executable PyTorch scripts across three prompt tiers of increasing specificity. These configurations were evaluated over 20 independent runs on a purpose-built dataset of 972 balanced images, using six classification metrics, four prompt quality metrics, and three resource efficiency dimensions. Ten of the twelve configurations converged to a high-performance plateau (accuracy 0.957-−0.967, AUC 0.985-−0.993). Claude at Tier 1 achieved the highest accuracy (0.967) and the lowest CPU usage (12.2%), whereas the best-calibrated (lowest-loss) pipelines were produced by Gemini and Grok at Tier 1 (test loss 0.127 and 0.142), reflecting an accuracy–calibration dissociation that we analyze in detail. However, Gemini and Grok experienced catastrophic convergence failures at Tier 3 (accuracy $$\approx $$ 0.58), revealing that over-specification of architectural and training constraints can destabilize CNN generation even when the produced scripts are syntactically valid. Higher prompt specificity does not consistently improve accuracy or validity rate. Instead, LLM identity interacts strongly with the prompt tier and emerges as a more critical factor than prompt design alone, although each LLM–tier condition is represented by a single generated script. Within the scope of this controlled, image-level evaluation, basic and structured prompting represent the recommended operating range for developing PPE compliance classifiers, delivering competitive accuracy and full validity rate across all models without the convergence failures observed at Tier 3. Validation in real industrial settings remains necessary.

candidates.title: A systematic workflow for utilizing and evaluating large language models in public health policy framing analysis
candidates.abstract: Abstract Background For public health policy research, it is crucial to monitor policy debates to inform evidence-based policymaking. One popular method is to analyze the news for salient frames used to argue for or against a controversial topic. However, this method is time and resource-intensive since domain experts need to manually analyze relevant articles to identify frames. This study presents an approach for using large language models (LLMs) to extract frames and to systematically evaluate results. Methods Building on the results of a framing analysis of the German media debate about a tax on animal-based foods, we developed a systematic workflow to utilize LLMs to extract all instances of the 10 most frequent manually coded negative frames from 46 news articles. With one prompt per article in a few-shot setting we generated a list of quote/frame pairs. We then evaluated results against human-coded ones and calculated precision, recall, and F1-score. Results GPT-5 achieved 79.8% precision and 79.8% recall, identifying 75.2% of manually coded frames. Extracted quotes generally aligned with human-extracted text sections. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview yielded higher precision but lower recall, resulting in a comparable F1-score (79.0% vs. 79.8% with GPT-5). These findings suggest the approach is generalizable across different frontier models. Conclusions This study introduces a workflow for LLM-assisted frame extraction and transparent evaluation against an expert reference standard. Integrating this approach into public health policy coding can save resources and accelerate analysis. Ultimately, this could increase the representativeness and timeliness of data, enhancing our understanding of ongoing public health policy debates.

candidates.title: Towards Agentic Agent-Based Models: Feasibility, Performance, and Statistical Model Checking
candidates.abstract: Abstract Agent-based models (ABMs) rely on simple, explicit and reproducible rules for individual decision making, while complex collective behavior emerges from interactions among agents. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) make it tempting to replace, enrich, or perturb these rules with LLM-based agentic capabilities. However, this raises a methodological question: how does introducing LLM-driven decisions affect the reliability, computational cost, and behavior of ABM simulations? We investigate this for Mesa ABM models, a popular Python library for ABMs, analyzed by statistical model checking. Building on Mesa’s integration with the statistical model checker MultiVeStA, we extend the classical Schelling segregation model with a hybrid population: ordinary agents classify neighbors using the standard symbolic rule, while one agent delegates this task to an LLM through tool calls. The LLM-enabled agent receives natural-language descriptions of neighboring agents and invokes tools that increment counters of similar/different neighbors; these counters determine its happiness according to the original Schelling dynamics. This provides a minimal but controlled setting where the semantic, operational, and computational behavior of LLM-based decisions can be studied inside an otherwise standard ABM. We report preliminary experiments with locally served LLMs of different sizes, showing that smaller models may fail simple semantic classification experiments or become operationally unusable during repeated tool-call generation, while larger tested models pass these preliminary checks. We discuss how statistical model checking can estimate classical ABM observables and quantify the impact of introducing agentic LLM components into simulation models.

candidates.title: Provable Coordination for LLM Agents via Message Sequence Charts
candidates.abstract: Abstract Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are difficult to reason about. Coordination errors such as deadlocks or type-mismatched messages are often hard to detect through testing. We introduce a domain-specific language for specifying agent coordination based on message sequence charts (MSCs). The language separates message-passing structure from LLM calls, tool calls, and human control points, whose outcomes remain unpredictable. We define the syntax and semantics of the language and present a syntax-directed projection that generates deadlock-free local agent programs from global coordination specifications. We illustrate the approach with a diagnosis consensus protocol and show how coordination properties can be established independently of LLM nondeterminism. We also describe a runtime planning extension in which an LLM dynamically generates a coordination workflow for which the same structural guarantees apply. An open-source Python implementation of our framework is available as ZipperGen.

candidates.title: Exploring the attitudinal effects of a personality-based de-escalation training program: Findings from the National De-escalation Training Center
candidates.abstract: Several high-profile incidents of police misconduct in the past decade have led to calls for reform and the prioritization of de-escalation training for law enforcement. However, the empirical evidence on various de-escalation strategies is in relative infancy. To further this scholarship, the current research represents a preliminary evaluation of the National De-escalation Training Center (NDTC) across several agencies and geographic regions of the United States. The study uses pre- and post-training data from over 500 trainees in the 6-month study period to determine if exposure to training informs changes to attitudes regarding procedural justice and de-escalation concepts. Factor analysis of the survey’s constructs and pre-post attitudinal change comparisons were conducted. Findings confirm that exposure to NDTC training resulted in significant improvements to procedural justice attitudes. Implications for in-service training and future research on long-term attitudinal change are explored.

candidates.title: Development of a Formal Training Program for Pharmacy Technicians to Assist in a Pediatric Medical Emergency Response
candidates.abstract: The development and evaluation of a formal training program designed to prepare pharmacy technicians to assist pharmacists during pediatric medical emergency responses is described. A structured training program was implemented at a pediatric hospital including didactic instruction, hands-on training, and a required return demonstration. Training emphasized medication preparation, labeling, automated dispensing system use, identification of emergency medications, and preparation of weight-based pediatric doses. Post-training survey results demonstrated improvements across all measured domains. Implementation of a formal pharmacy technician training program improved technician confidence in emergency response medications while supporting effective performance during pediatric medical emergencies.

candidates.title: The Impact of Retrieval Augmented Generation on the Reliability of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency but remain fundamentally unreliable for knowledge-intensive tasks due to hallucination, temporal staleness, and lack of verifiability.Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant architectural paradigm that grounds generation in external evidence.This paper provides a comprehensive investigation into how RAG reshapes LLM reliability across factual accuracy, citation fidelity, temporal freshness, and robustness to noise.We benchmark five RAG variants against closed-book baselines using secondary datasets including Natural Questions, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and RGB.Results show an average 23.7% reduction in hallucination rate and 31.2%improvement in citation grounding when using advanced retrieval with self-reflection.However, we identify critical failure modes: retriever-generator misalignment, context distraction, and over-reliance on irrelevant passages.We propose a reliability framework and demonstrate that corrective and modular RAG designs significantly mitigate these risks.Our findings establish RAG as necessary but not sufficient for trustworthy deployment.

candidates.title: BanglaDiaHallu: Hallucinations of large language models and the effect of guideline-grounded retrieval-augmented generation in Bangla diabetes question answering
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for health advice, but they can produce fluent statements that are false or unsupported, known as hallucinations, and this risk is poorly characterised in low-resource languages such as Bangla. We measured hallucinations of locally deployable open-weight LLMs in Bangla diabetes question answering and tested whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounded in Bangladesh’s National Guideline on Diabetes Mellitus reduces them. Forty patient questions spanning six clinical sub-domains were each answered twice, under zero-shot prompting, by Qwen3.5-9B, TigerLLM-9B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, and by BanglaDiaRAG, which adds hybrid dense (BGE-M3) and sparse (BM25) retrieval from a physician-reviewed Bangla guideline knowledge base to Qwen3.5-9B. Two physicians rated the 400 de-identified responses by consensus for medical accuracy, completeness, safety, readability and reliability on a 0–1 scale, and responses with accuracy below 0.70 were classified as hallucinated. Hallucination rates were 2.5% for Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3.8% for TigerLLM-9B, 22.5% for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and 77.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Guideline grounding lowered the rate of Qwen3.5-9B to 11.3% (difference −66.3 percentage points; 95% CI −76.3 to −55.0) and raised every criterion by 0.24 to 0.38 points (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). BanglaDiaRAG outscored Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on all five criteria and matched or exceeded TigerLLM-9B, but it remained below Gemma-4-26B-A4B in safety, readability and reliability, and its residual errors were specific, confident and potentially harmful. Guideline grounding can turn a weak general-purpose model into a much safer Bangla diabetes assistant, but the choice of base model mattered as much as retrieval and no configuration was free of hallucination, so clinical oversight remains essential before patient-facing use.

candidates.title: Structured Workflows and Retrieval-Augmented Generation Improve LLM Recommendations for Colorectal Liver Metastases: The METATRON Study
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) show promise for clinical decision support, but their ability to reproduce multidisciplinary oncologic reasoning is unclear. We evaluated whether structured clinical workflows and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve concordance between LLM-generated and expert reference recommendations across 110 synthetic colorectal liver metastasis (CRLM) vignettes spanning eight clinical scenarios. Four inference strategies built on the same LLM (gpt-oss-120B)—baseline prompting, RAG, workflow-guided prompting, and their combination (WF-RAG-LLM)—were scored by three independent LLM judges across five dimensions. WF-RAG-LLM achieved the highest aggregated score (0.626 ± 0.070), ahead of RAG-LLM (0.559 ± 0.111), WF-LLM (0.527 ± 0.168), and baseline (0.444 ± 0.162), with the largest gains in post-chemotherapy, recurrent, and anatomically challenging scenarios. Combining expert-derived workflow guidance with retrieval-based knowledge grounding achieved the highest overall concordance with expert reference recommendations, supporting clinically informed reasoning architecture as an important component of LLM performance in complex oncologic decision support.

candidates.title: Towards Next-Generation Architectures of Large Language Models: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly through increases in model scale, data, and computation, while their underlying architectures have also undergone substantial evolution. Beyond the canonical Transformer architecture, recent designs seek greater efficiency, scalability, and flexibility by rethinking how sequence information is processed, represented, and transformed. We survey efficient attention and state management, modern recurrent and other linear-complexity sequence models, Mixture-of-Experts architectures, and advances in activation functions, normalization, residual connections, positional encoding, and tokenization. We also cover multi-token prediction and adaptive and recurrent depth. Across these areas, we highlight key design principles and trade-offs among representational power, optimization stability, and computational cost. Complementing this component-wise treatment, we take a system-level perspective. We trace representative open-weight LLM families to identify recurring patterns in how architectural choices are combined, and synthesize these developments along four dimensions—processing structure, transformation dynamics, state management, and output commitment—characterizing how recent designs preserve, refine, or relax the assumptions of the canonical decoder. Together, this survey aims to provide a systematic overview of LLM architectural evolution and to chart pathways toward next-generation designs.

candidates.title: Detecting Health Misinformation Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model
candidates.abstract: Misinformation is common in online media, including in health-related content. Such misinformation constitutes a significant risk to the medical-demographic security of the population. Many people actively seek medical information online without the ability to verify its trustworthiness. This paper proposes a modular system for automated detection of misinformation in medical content based on retrieval-augmented verification. In the pipeline, input articles are summarized and decomposed into atomic claims. Each claim is then vectorized using dense embeddings (BGE-Large-en-v1.5) and matched against a self-constructed knowledge base via cosine similarity to retrieve evidence. Retrieved evidence is verified using large language model (LLM)- based natural language inference (NLI) and aggregated into article-level predictions through a scoring function. The LLM used in the system is the open-source LLaMA-3.1 model with eight billion parameters. Together with a self-contained knowledge base, this represents a deliberately constrained environment. Such a setup isolates the contribution of the presented architecture from its dependency on external knowledge sources and LLMs with large parameter counts. The system achieved 98.4% accuracy and a macro F1 of 0.978 at 79.0% coverage on the evaluated datasets (DETERRENT and CONSTRAINT). This demonstrates that, even under resource constraints, the correct pipeline architecture enables high-precision misinformation detection on medical content. It also represents a clear improvement over the ablation experiment, which used the same model without the proposed pipeline and achieved an F1 of only 0.773.

candidates.title: A Comparative Analysis of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering, summarisation, coding, and research support, yet choosing a suitable model remains difficult because models differ in performance, context capacity, cost, privacy, and deployment options. This paper presents a document-based comparative analysis of five LLMs: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 405B Instruct, and Mistral Large 2. Using published technical reports, official documentation, model cards, and recognised benchmark studies, the models are examined under a common framework covering response quality, reasoning, coding, language understanding, context-window capacity, speed, computational requirements, cost, privacy, and deployment flexibility. No new experiments are conducted, and results obtained under different evaluation conditions are not treated as directly equivalent. The analysis shows that model selection involves trade-offs: hosted models offer easier access, whereas models with downloadable weights give greater deployment control but require more computing resources. No single model is found to be best for every task, which supports a task-specific approach to selecting LLMs.

candidates.title: Adaptive Code Generation for Controlling Robots
candidates.abstract: Abstract Deploying robots as Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS) in unknown and dynamic environments necessitates a transition from rigid command libraries toward intention-based autonomy, as natural language represents the only medium capable of articulating complex goals beyond the capacity of finite instruction sets. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a path toward natural language goal description, their integration introduces significant challenges: the formalization gap between imprecise intentions and executable actions, the taxonomy gap induced by unpredictable environments, and the challenge of maintaining temporal state and progress awareness. This work introduces an architectural framework that enables robotic control by leveraging generative AI. The system follows a dual-AI design: an LLM translates high-level intentions into executable program code restricted to a formal robotic library and constrained by verifiable syntax, while a Vision-Language Model (VLM) provides semantic grounding via a distillation process. To ensure robustness, the framework incorporates environment-driven replanning triggers based on geometric and semantic thresholds, complemented by continuous runtime monitoring and an adaptive planning loop. Benchmarked across frontier models, our framework architecture demonstrates that grounding generative AI in a reactive, constrained loop enables robust fulfillment of complex intentions in dynamic and unknown environments.

candidates.title: An Integrated ETL–OLAP and Semantic Retrieval Architecture for Hybrid Analysis of Structured and Unstructured Enterprise Data
candidates.abstract: Extract, Transform, and Load (ETL) and Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) provide robust mechanisms for integrating structured data and supporting multidimensional analysis. Still, they offer limited support for semantic access to unstructured textual content. This study proposes an integrated architecture that combines conventional ETL and data warehousing with semantic retrieval based on dense vector representations and similarity search. The architecture separates structured analytical processing from semantic document retrieval while preserving traceability among source documents, warehouse records, and vector representations. The architecture was examined through an implementation-oriented case study using a large document collection of up to 1.58 million PDF files. The study reports descriptive implementation observations on data ingestion, vector indexing, and query execution in the deployed environment. These observations characterize the operational behavior of the implemented system and are not presented as a controlled performance benchmark between OLAP and semantic retrieval, because the two mechanisms address different classes of information needs. The architecture also provides a query-time foundation for downstream Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); however, this study does not assess generative response quality or LLM orchestration as case-study outcomes. Accordingly, this work contributes primarily through the architectural integration of structured analytical processing and semantic retrieval, preservation of document-to-warehouse-to-vector traceability, and practical implementation of the framework over a large enterprise document repository. The study also identifies limitations related to repeated timing measurements, stage-level profiling, independently annotated relevance judgments, and retrieval-effectiveness assessment. These limitations define future work involving Precision@k, Recall@k, MRR, nDCG, controlled workload benchmarking, and systematic evaluation of RAG-generated responses.

candidates.title: Efficient and Effective Test Generation and Type Inference for Python Applications
candidates.abstract: Python has become one of the most widely used programming languages, valued for its flexibility and ease of use. However, its dynamic nature provides only limited static guarantees, making programs more difficult to write reliably: errors are more likely to remain undetected until runtime. Tests and type checking can mitigate these issues by detecting bugs—including runtime errors—before release, but creating tests and the type annotations required for checking demands substantial developer effort, discouraging their widespread use. Approaches to automating test generation and type inference are hindered not only by Python’s dynamic features but also by the substantial performance limitations of CPython, the standard Python interpreter, which make dynamic analysis costly in practice. In this dissertation, I explore how low-overhead dynamic analysis can be used to improve the reliability of Python software. First, I introduce SlipCover, a code coverage measurement tool that significantly reduces runtime overhead through efficient bytecode instrumentation and dynamic de-instrumentation. SlipCover enables practical use of coverage tracking in iterative workflows by achieving near-zero overhead, supporting a range of software engineering applications. Building on SlipCover, I next present CoverUp, a regression test generation tool that uses coverage feedback to efficiently guide a large language model in generating unit tests that significantly outperform previous methods in coverage. Finally, I propose RightTyper, an efficient and effective type annotation system. RightTyper combines types observed through low-overhead, statistically guided runtime sampling with static analysis and name resolution to produce type annotations comparable in quality to current LLM-based approaches and substantially better than those of all other evaluated tools—while remaining grounded in observed program behavior rather than probabilistic inference. Collectively, these contributions advance the state of the art by showing how low-overhead dynamic analysis helps overcome significant challenges in writing and maintaining reliable Python code.

candidates.title: Data Optimization for LLMs: A Survey
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted great attention in both academic and industrial communities in recent years. Numerous survey studies have covered various aspects of LLMs, such as learning strategies, applications, alignment, explainability, and evaluation. However, little headway has been made in reviewing data-related aspects for LLMs, despite data being recognized as a key factor contributing to the emergence of the LLMs era. A wide range of data optimization algorithms and techniques are employed in LLMs' training and application processes. These techniques often originate from diverse deep learning domains, with their theoretical inspirations and heuristic motivations appearing unrelated to each other. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for LLMs' data optimization techniques to enhance data utilization efficiency. We first discuss data challenges in LLMs' training and inference. Second, we summarize data perception dimensions for evaluating LLMs' data properties. Third, existing optimization techniques are reviewed and categorized into four groups: data selection, augmentation, reweighting, and others. Fourth, we analyze interconnections between these categories. Finally, we identify key challenges and future directions for LLMs' data optimization compared with conventional deep learning approaches.

candidates.title: Beyond Binary Rewrite Decisions: Separating Rewrite-Intensity Control from Level Prediction in a Frozen-LLM Generation-and-Selection Pipeline for Korean Easy-Read Drafting
candidates.abstract: Editors of published Korean Easy-Read documents changed 50 aligned sentences by widely varying amounts (edit distance 0.39–0.89), motivating rewrite intensity as a control variable for large language models (LLMs). We ask whether a requested intensity is realized per sentence and whether the level to request can be predicted from the source, using a generation-and-selection pipeline over a frozen LLM (EXAONE-3.5-7.8B-Instruct) in two sequential protocols with criteria hash-frozen before generation. Realized intensity is normalized character edit distance, which measures change, not readability, meaning preservation or Easy-Read quality. A four-level protocol (v1) ordered outputs on average but failed the sentence-level criterion (14/50 under its zero-tolerance rule). A three-level follow-up (v2), designed after that failure with several simultaneous changes, met its criterion for the whole pipeline, including its intensity-aware selector: 41/50 sources were non-decreasingly ordered at the declared tolerance (24/50 with strict increases; post hoc, 30/50 without the selector’s intensity-match term at that tolerance). Three runs of one LLM proxy perceived the ordering (consistency, not validity); no human evaluated the outputs. Stronger levels reduced source similarity without monotonically reducing lexical difficulty. Six source features did not support prediction of the LLM-proxy-preferred level under a pre-specified rule (quadratic-weighted κ −0.098 vs. 0.012), so no adaptive allocation was built. Rewrite-intensity control and level allocation therefore require separate validation.

candidates.title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.

candidates.title: Managing Vector Data for Retrieval Augmented Generation@Dagstuhl Seminar Summary
candidates.abstract: This report summarizes discussions that took place in the context of a Dagstuhl seminar1 to explore the emerging paradigm of AI-native databases designed to support agentic workflows and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with robust database abstractions. The central synthesis of the Dagstuhl discussions is the necessary evolution of databases from passive vector stores into active data-native agentic harnesses that orchestrate AI reasoning and task-centric execution. A recurring lesson across keynotes and working groups is that achieving mission-critical reliability requires integrating AI primitives, such as embeddings, model inference, and semantic operators, as first-class citizens while maintaining traditional database guarantees like transactional consistency, explainability, and cost-aware optimization. This transition necessitates a structured approach to agent memory (spanning episodic, semantic, and procedural scales) and a shift toward adaptive, iterative execution models that go beyond static query planning to accommodate the stochastic nature of foundation models. There is a community consensus that reliability, responsibility, and security (specifically addressing compositional leakage) must be treated as end-to-end concerns supported by holistic benchmarks that evaluate the entire quality chain from retrieval to autonomous action.

candidates.title: A Systematic Review of Hallucination Mitigation in Large Language Models Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become widely used for question answering, education, research, summarization and information support. Despite their usefulness, LLMs may generate false, unsupported or inconsistent information, commonly described as hallucination. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this reliability problem by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources and supplying it to the language model as contextual evidence before generating a response. This paper studies the role of RAG in reducing factual hallucinations through a review of existing research and a 50 question pilot comparison of responses generated with and without retrieval support. The submitted report records 49 of 50 responses as correct without RAG and all 50 as correct with RAG; it separately presents a clearly labelled illustrative distribution of 46/3/1 versus 48/2/0 for demonstrating response categories. The distinction is retained to avoid presenting illustrative values as observed experimental results. The study also examines limitations including poor retrieval, unreliable sources, incomplete context and incorrect interpretation of retrieved evidence. The paper concludes that RAG is a practical hallucination-reduction approach, but it should be combined with high-quality retrieval, evidence verification and human oversight for critical applications.

candidates.title: Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by querying external structured knowledge. However, it can also introduce privacy risks by leaking sensitive information from the retrieval datastore. We propose a simple method to preserve datastore privacy in RAG systems via random projection. By applying the same projection to both datastore embeddings and query embeddings, our method provably preserves semantic similarity between queries and retrieved items while substantially mitigating data extraction attacks. Across multiple RAG architectures and datasets, we show that this lightweight approach achieves superior retrieval and generation performance compared to prior methods which leverage formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees, while exhibiting comparable empirical privacy under strong attack models. Our results for the first time suggest that random projection can serve as a competitive and practical baseline for privacy-preserving RAG systems.

candidates.title: KBS: A Korean Benchmark Suite for Foundation Model Evaluation
candidates.abstract: We present a Korean Benchmark Suite (KBS) comprising Ko-ARC, Ko-GSM8K, Ko-EQ-Bench, Ko-WinoGrande, Ko-LAMBADA, and Ko-IFEval, covering six capabilities across 9,396 items. The suite combines review, localization, direct Korean construction, and redesign for Korean, avoiding a translation-only approach to benchmark adaptation. We evaluate Korean-developed models, multilingual open models, and closed API models under protocols that account for model access, prompt format, and scoring differences. Results show that Korean benchmark scores depend on task construction, scoring rules, prompting, and model post-training. These findings suggest that Korean evaluation should report both final scores and the settings used to obtain them.

candidates.title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): An Adaptive Framework for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering
candidates.abstract: This paper presents a proposed Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded question answering using large language models (LLMs). Unlike conventional single-pass RAG systems, the proposed framework incorporates query planning, retrieval, tool selection, evidence evaluation, answer generation, and self-reflection. The framework uses a bounded feedback loop to improve evidence retrieval when the initial results are insufficient or conflicting. It aims to produce answers supported by relevant source citations while communicating uncertainty when reliable evidence is unavailable. The paper discusses the system architecture, workflow, algorithmic control logic, evaluation methodology, security, privacy, and governance considerations. It also proposes evaluation metrics for answer quality, retrieval effectiveness, factual grounding, latency, computational cost, and component-level ablation studies. Potential applications include research assistance, document question answering, enterprise knowledge management, customer support, and data analysis. This work presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation plan. Implementation, benchmark experiments, and measured performance improvements are not reported. Keywords: Agentic RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, Adaptive Retrieval, Self-Reflection.

candidates.title: From Long Context to Selective Memory:A Survey of Memory-Centric Compression for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Long-context capability has become essential for large language models (LLMs) to handle complex tasks, yet continuously expanding the context window does not remove the computational, storage, and information-selection pressures incurred at inference time. Existing work on prompt compression, KV-cache management, efficient serving, retrieval augmentation, and agent memory is usually discussed in isolation, leaving the flow of information between storage and computation insufficiently understood. This survey reframes long-context compression as a memory-management problem for allocating inference-time resources. We distinguish compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation, from compute-inactive memory, which lies outside the computation path but can be stored, retrieved, updated, or forgotten, and we characterize offloaded KV caches, persistent prefix caches, and precomputed KV states as intermediate states on the activation path. On this basis, we formulate writing, offloading, recall, retrieval-and-injection, materialization, eviction, consolidation, and forgetting as state transitions within an information lifecycle, and introduce a budgeted cost model that places these operations in a single cost account. The resulting framework unifies short-term context compression, long-term memory management, and the transitions between them, and shows that the central challenge is not merely reducing information volume but deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form. We further summarize evaluation dimensions, benchmark gaps, and open challenges, and argue that future research should move from static, pointwise compression toward dynamic, governable, lifecycle-aware memory management.

candidates.title: Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
candidates.abstract: One of the first steps of a research pipeline is generating ideas. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate this step, but most of this work optimizes the quality of individual ideas, while overlooking diversity. In our work, we study document-grounded ideation, focusing on increasing the diversity of LLM generated ideas and ensuring they are high quality. Given prior papers, a model must propose a set of ideas that are each high-quality and clearly distinct from one another, while also being grounded in the input documents. To optimize for this, we propose training with a set-level reinforcement learning objective. In our setup, in a single generation, the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in the source papers, and the set is scored jointly, where each idea's quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas written before it. This teaches the model to steer each new idea away from its predecessors. We show that our trained 8B model achieves higher creative utility (a measure combining quality and diversity) than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-6 Astra on our contamination-free benchmark. In a pilot human study with four experts, our sets are judged as promising as Claude Opus 4.8's and contain marginally more unique ideas. When a coding agent runs proof-of-concept experiments on the ideas, our model's success@k is comparable to Claude Opus 4.8's, so we see that the added diversity does not cost any executability.

candidates.title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.

candidates.title: Data Strategies for Large Language Models: A Unified Perspective on the Training Lifecycle
candidates.abstract: Data strategy plays a central role in training large language models (LLMs). It governs the selection, weighting, and scheduling of training data, thereby determining the capabilities a model can acquire from a fixed data budget. We treat high-quality data as having high training-dependent utility, which depends on the target objective, the model, and its training state rather than on the text alone. Research in this area now spans pretraining and post-training, but related ideas use inconsistent terminology and evaluation protocols. This work reviews data strategies across the training lifecycle and formulates them as policies that allocate a training budget over candidate examples. We organise methods by their decision granularity, model dependence, and temporal adaptivity, then compare their computational requirements and empirical support. Fine-grained or state-dependent policies offer more control but incur additional scoring, search, or rollout costs. Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end-to-end cost remains limited. A continuously updated list of papers, along with their public implementations, is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/data_strategy_survey.

candidates.title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.

candidates.title: Loud and Clear: Making Visual Evidence Count in Multimodal Document RAG
candidates.abstract: Multimodal document retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has focused largely on retrieval, yet its answers depend on how well a vision-language model reads the retrieved pages. We find that evidence in retrieved pages remains underused even when the correct pages are retrieved. On SciEGQA oracle pages, five prior methods give the generator 0.7K to 2.7K visual tokens per query on average under a common image processor, yet raising the page-only budget from 1K to 32K improves accuracy by 15.22 points. At a fixed 16K budget, adding ground-truth crops improves accuracy by 3.75 points over page-only input. We study what the generator needs from retrieved pages through two requirements: Loud, making full use of visual token capacity, and Clear, refining the page so that its evidence becomes prominent. For Loud, increasing either the visual token budget or visual fidelity, the image resolution those tokens preserve, improves accuracy with the other held fixed, and full-page scaling outperforms repetition and tiling at matched budgets. For Clear, suppressing surrounding content improves accuracy without enlarging selected regions, and adding OCR of these regions to page images outperforms either input alone. We implement both as Loud and Clear (LoC), which combines higher-resolution pages with OCR from query-relevant regions without ground-truth annotations or additional training. LoC outperforms eight prior methods on SciEGQA, ViDoRe-v3, and MMLongBench-Doc, improving over the strongest, ColQwen3, by 8.88, 3.09, and 4.22 points with the same retriever and generator. It also outperforms its page-only variant under the same visual token budget. These results locate a bottleneck beyond retrieval: how the retrieved pages are given to the generator.

candidates.title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.

The evaluation dataset consists of 514 Bengali legal scenarios categorized into Natural Language, Legal Language, Factual, and Out of Context types. Each scenario is annotated with corresponding gold legal references to support the evaluation of legal information retrieval and question-answering systems. The dataset is intended to facilitate research on Bengali legal NLP, evidence-based legal retrieval, RAG pipelines, and the development and evaluation of legal question-answering systems in the Bangladeshi legal context.

candidates.abstract: The use of textbooks as primary sources of information has increasingly given way to tools based on Large Language Models (LLMs), raising concerns about the reliability of generated answers. This study investigates how different adaptation strategies shape the behavior of small language models in educational Question Answering (QA) tasks in Portuguese. To support this analysis, we built a question-answer dataset derived from an NLP textbook and compared base models and the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline with models adapted through supervised fine-tuning and Continued Pretraining. The evaluation relies on questions from the LARI dataset, which has been validated by human specialists, and combines automatic and qualitative assessment procedures. The findings indicate that small models tuned with structured instructional knowledge achieve stronger semantic alignment and produce more pertinent answers in Portuguese educational QA scenarios.

candidates.title: Rethinking the Role of Tool Graph Memory in Multi-Turn Tool Use
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.

candidates.title: Multi-sourced AI Tutor for Non-Native English Speaker Students
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted as teaching tools in computing education, particularly for developing AI tutors capable of answering student questions. With the rise in enrollment of international students in computing programs, researchers have begun to explore the difficulties that non-native English speaker (NNES) students face in computing courses due to language barriers. To aid such students, we developed a general-purpose AI tutor system that can process student questions in foreign languages (currently focused on Mandarin) and provide bilingual responses. Our system also incorporates the functionality of generating a glossary of technical terms and their explanations to enhance comprehension. Our approach utilizes a specialized Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline with a novel question extraction mechanism, enabling us to effectively utilize a diverse array of course materials for answering student queries. We evaluated our AI tutor using 91 Piazza posts, demonstrating that it could answer 83.52% of the posts correctly and in a helpful manner. The tutor also provided high-quality translations for 76.92% of the questions and generated technical term glossaries for 64.47% of them. Our findings underscore the potential of multi-source RAG pipeline in enhancing AI tutor systems, offering support for non-native speakers that are challenging to provide with traditional supporting staff of a computing course.

candidates.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries
candidates.abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.

candidates.title: Incentivizing Tool-Use Reinforcement Learning for Post-Arrival Emergency Care Prediction
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reason over both structured measurements and free-text records, which makes them attractive for emergency department (ED) prediction. However, most existing LLMs still fall short of conventional ML methods like trees on EHR-based prediction tasks. Our controlled analysis traces this gap to two weaknesses: LLMs do not select informative features, and they misjudge what numerical values imply for risk even when given the right features. We propose TIR-EC, a tool-integrated reinforcement learning framework that addresses both. TIR-EC exposes EHR feature groups as tools the LLM can call. It trains the LLM with rewards from a gradient-boosted tree teacher, which provides a reference set of informative tools and a graded risk target. TIR-EC also distills task-specific clinical skills into the model weights through a reverse curriculum that gradually removes the skills from the prompt during RL process. Evaluation on three clinical prediction tasks shows that our 4B agent achieves the highest macro F1 of all compared models, outperforms conventional ML baselines, and is competitive with much larger frontier LLMs. Further analysis shows that TIR-EC selects more useful evidence with fewer tool calls and combines measurements more effectively.

candidates.title: CART: Compatible Routing for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance through instruction tuning, yet real-world applications often require them to continually acquire new capabilities from sequential tasks, i.e., Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). In typical MLLMs, a projector is employed to align visual representations with the language model. However, existing methods primarily protect the language model from forgetting while continuously updating the projector across tasks. Such asymmetric adaptation can cause substantial representation drift in the projector, increasing the mismatch between the projector and language model and consequently exacerbating catastrophic forgetting. To address this issue, we propose Compatible Routing (CART), which explicitly coordinates the adaptation of the projector and language model. Specifically, CART maintains task-specific experts for both modules and combines them through weighted mixtures. CART jointly infers their weights by considering both expert relevance and cross-module compatibility, thereby promoting coordinated adaptation between the two modules. To further control model growth, we introduce relevance-guided expert consolidation, which merges experts exhibiting similar relevance profiles across samples within each module. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CART achieves state-of-the-art performance.

candidates.title: When Reasoning Is Not Enough: Proactive Inquiry for Cross-Modal Safety in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can act unsafely when individually benign images and texts are interpreted jointly. Beyond implicit reasoning risk, where reasoning drifts toward harm, we identify intent-level risk, where cross-modal ambiguity silently commits the model to a hazardous premise that path-level optimization alone cannot correct. We propose SAFE-PRO, which uses a Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty (RCU) signal, combining predictive entropy with a learned cross-modal risk score, to decide when to ask safety-grounded clarifying questions and where to apply path optimization, under a reward that prioritizes safety and penalizes over-refusal. We also build SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision, and theoretically analyze gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk under RCU. Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, SAFE-PRO consistently improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves its over-refusal, and surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.

candidates.title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation
candidates.abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.

candidates.title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On $τ^2$-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic.

candidates.title: Tool-Augmented Large Language Models for Reliable Medical Calculation from Patient Notes
candidates.abstract: Medical calculators translate raw patient observations into clinically actionable values and scores. However, applying these calculators directly to free-form patient notes requires precise variable extraction combined with the exact execution of complex formulas, scoring rules, and output conventions. Relying solely on direct large language model (LLM) prompting is unreliable in this context, as rule recall, parameter extraction, arithmetic reasoning, and formatting become entangled within a single generative step. To address these limitations, we propose a tool-augmented LLM framework for reliable medical calculation from patient notes. The framework retrieves and structures calculator specifications, generates reusable executable tools, and uses a constrained extractor to map each patient note to calculator-ready inputs. The tools then perform deterministic calculation, separating clinical language understanding from rule execution and arithmetic. Evaluated on the MedCalc-Bench dataset, our method achieves 86.73% final-answer accuracy, outperforming the one-shot prompting and supervised fine tuning-only baselines by 24.0 and 17.27 percentage points. Ablation and error analyses show that these performance gains are primarily driven by rule-grounded tool synthesis and schema-constrained extraction, whereas remaining failures are concentrated in clinical-semantic extraction and benchmark-specific output contracts. By grounding calculator logic in executable tools, the proposed approach alleviates arithmetic hallucinations and improves the computational reliability of the final clinical outputs.

candidates.title: The Density of Thought: Predicting and Steering Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.

candidates.title: Progress Reward Model for Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PRM4RL.

candidates.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
candidates.abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.
